spans.content: Ligand-Controlled Preparation of Aryl-Substituted Allenes Enabled
by Nickel-Catalyzed Reductive Coupling of Secondary Propargylic
Carbonates with Aryl Halides
Ruotong Li, Jie Hu, Yonghao Xi, Hegui Gong,* and Weichen Huang*
ABSTRACT: Herein, we developed a new method for the synthesis of aryl-substituted allenes through a nickel-catalyzed reductive
coupling reaction between secondary propargyl carbonates and aryl halides. By employing the dimethyl-1,10-phenanthroline ligand,
we achieved a ligand-controlled, regioselective nickel-catalyzed reductive arylation, overcoming the structural limitations of propargyl
electrophiles. Notably, this reaction exhibits exceptional functional group compatibility, rendering it particularly suitable for late-
stage allenylation modifications of complex molecules.

s key cumulated dienes, allenes have attracted attention in
pharmaceutical and synthetic chemistry for their unique
biological and chemical properties.<sup>1</sup> They are present in
naturally occurring bioactive molecules and also serve as
versatile building blocks in organic synthesis, facilitating
complex molecule construction.<sup>1−3</sup> Among the numerous
strategies devised for the synthesis of allenes,<sup>4</sup> the transition-
metal-catalyzed cross-coupling of propargyl electrophiles with
diverse aryl nucleophiles has emerged as a reliable and efective
approach to aryl-substituted allenes (Scheme 1A).<sup>5</sup> However,
this classic approach faces the following challenges: (1) the
narrow scope of aryl organometallic nucleophiles; (2) poor
regioselectivity between propargylic and allenyl substitution;
(3) low functional group compatibilities and application values.
As a result, there remains a need to explore more eficient
synthetic methods to address the limitations of conventional
nucleophile-involved coupling processes.
Recently, nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling reactions have
gained recognition in both academia and industry as an
alternative to traditional coupling reactions. By directly
employing stable, readily available organic halides, these
reactions simplify synthetic operations, and avoids the need
for metal reagent preparations.<sup>6</sup> In this context, nickel-catalyzed
reductive coupling of propargyl electrophiles with various alkyl
electrophiles has been advanced for practical synthesis of alkyl
substituted allenes (Scheme 1B).<sup>7</sup> In contrast, preparation of
aryl-substituted allenes through similar nickel-catalyzed reduc-

Ligand-Controlled Preparation of Aryl-Substituted Allenes Enabled
by Nickel-Catalyzed Reductive Coupling of Secondary Propargylic
Carbonates with Aryl Halides
Ruotong Li, Jie Hu, Yonghao Xi, Hegui Gong,* and Weichen Huang*

Herein, we disclosed our success in the development of an
unprecedented ligand-controlled regioselective nickel-catalyzed
reductive arylation of C3-secondary propargyl electrophiles,
ofering an eficient approach to C1-arylated allenes in high
eficiency, and providing a solution to previously unaddressed
substrate-dependent regioselectivity issue. By employing readily
accessible aryl halides, this method facilitates the synthesis of
structurally varied aryl-substituted allenes, demonstrating
remarkable regioselectivity and broad substrate compatibility
(Scheme 1D).
We evaluated various substrates with diferent leaving groups
and identified propargyl phenyl carbonate 1a as the optimal
template substrate for the reaction (see SI for details). Next, we
investigated the reaction conditions for the nickel-catalyzed
reductive coupling reaction between propargyl phenyl carbonate
1a and aryl halide 2a, with detailed results outlined in Table 1.
Our primary focus was on exploring the modulating efects of
various ligands on the regioselectivity of the reaction (Table 1,
entries 1−8). Screening of a series of parameters has revealed
that the choice of ligand has a significant impact on the
regioselectivity of the reaction, particularly in terms of the steric
hindrance efect around the nickel center. Specifically, in
scenarios where the nickel center is surrounded by a more
crowded environment, it exhibits a propensity to promote the
formation of allene products, which is largely consistent with our
initial conception. Further analysis revealed that bipyridine
ligands L2 and L3, difering in the position of their methyl
groups, displayed vastly diferent regioselectivity in facilitating
the reaction (Table 1, entries 2−3). Despite achieving an
excellent regioselectivity ratio of 9:1 with the use of ligand L3,
the overall reaction yield remained around 20%. Based on these
insights, we conducted a more rigorous screening of ligands.
Ultimately, dimethyl-1,10-phenanthroline L6 was chosen as the
optimal ligand as it efectively balances a certain level ofregiosel-
ectivity with a notable improvement in the overall reaction
eficiency (Table 1, entry 6). It is worth noting that despite the
potential for even better regioselectivity ofered by L8 as a ligand
due to its larger steric hindrance, its lower overall reaction
eficiency made it a less favorable choice (Table 1, entry 8).
Subsequently, we further examined diferent types of nickel
sources, solvents, and bases. Ultimately, with the positively
cooperative efects of
\mathrm { N i I } _ { 2 }
and
{ \mathrm { N a H C O } } _ { 3 } ,
we confirmed the
optimal reaction conditions, yielding aryl-substituted allene
products with a yield of 95%, while the production of propargylic
products was almost completely suppressed (Table 1, entry 12).
Under the optimized reaction conditions, substitution of aryl
iodides with aryl bromides led to significantly diminished yields,
while no desired product was observed when employing aryl
chlorides (Table 1, entries 13 and 14).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we further
investigated the scope of aryl halides. As shown in Scheme 2, a
series of aryl iodides bearing either electron-withdrawing groups
or electron-donating groups underwent smooth with secondary
propargylic carbonate 1a or 1b, afording aryl-substituted allenes
3a−3o in moderate to good yields and remarkable regiose-
lectivity. Notably, a diverse array of functional groups, including
esters (3a, 3l), thioethers (3b), acetyl (3c), cyano (3d), fluorine
(3e), amides (3f, 3g), carbonyls (3i), chlorine (3j), and
trifluoromethyl (3o), were all found compatible in the standard
method (Scheme 2). However, aryl halides with ortho-
substituents exhibited a pronounced decrease in yield,

in moderate to good yields. This
highlights the robustness and broad applicability of the present

to demonstrate the practical applicability of this method, we
applied it to the late-stage diversification of complex molecules.
Remarkably, the coupling reaction between secondary prop-
argylic phenyl carbonate 1b and Estrone, Flurbiprofen, Isoxepac,

The robustness of this allene-forming reaction was further
demonstrated by a gram-scale synthesis of 4 in high yield and
regioselectivity (Scheme 4A). Interestingly, the reaction is also
applicable to alkenyl electrophiles, which furnished alkenyl-
substituted allene 5 in moderate yield, without encountering
appreciable amount of the alkynylation byproduct (Scheme 4B).
Following this achievement, we assessed the stereoselectivity of
the reaction. When utilizing the commercial Pybox ligand L9,
product 3h demonstrated a notable level of stereoselectivity,
hinting at the potential feasibility of nickel-catalyzed reductive
coupling for the preparation of chiral allenes (Scheme 4C).
Finally, the synthetic versatility of the aryl-substituted allenes
was demonstrated through a series of postsynthetic trans-
formations. Upon treatment of 4 with tetrabutylammonium
fluoride

in the presence of 2-bromobenzaldehyde, the
transient allenyl alcohol was formed, which was immediately
oxidized to the ketone 6 (Scheme 4D). Furthermore, 3h
underwent eficient desil- ylation to aford a disubstituted allene
compound 7. By employing the C−H bond activation method
developed by the Liu research

To gain insight into the reaction details, we first investigated
whether a radical pathway is involved in the reaction. Although
no radical-trapped products were detected, the presence of two
equivalents of the radical scavenger TEMPO inhibited the
reaction to a certain extent (Scheme 5A). Furthermore, the
addition of 1,1-diphenylethylene had a negligible impact on the
reaction eficiency (Scheme 5A). Additionally, when a substrate
bearing the cyclopropane radical clock was tested, the allene
product 9 was formed without ring opening (Scheme 5B). The
collective results suggest that the reaction likely does not
proceed via a radical pathway, in contrast to previous nickel-
catalyzed coupling reactions of propargyl eletrophiles.<sup>[8][9][10b]</sup>

To gain insight into the reaction details, we first investigated
whether a radical pathway is involved in the reaction. Although
no radical-trapped products were detected, the presence of two
equivalents of the radical scavenger TEMPO inhibited the
reaction to a certain extent (Scheme 5A). Furthermore, the
addition of 1,1-diphenylethylene had a negligible impact on the
reaction eficiency (Scheme 5A). Additionally, when a substrate
bearing the cyclopropane radical clock was tested, the allene
product 9 was formed without ring opening (Scheme 5B). The
collective results suggest that the reaction likely does not
proceed via a radical pathway, in contrast to previous nickel-
catalyzed coupling reactions of propargyl eletrophiles.<sup>[8][9][10b]</sup>

gain a deeper understanding of the reaction mechanism

observed. This discovery suggests that the oxidative addition
reaction of propargyl carbonate may be initiated by a nickel(I)
intermediate. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that no allenyl self-
coupling products were detected throughout the reaction
process, further suggesting that the formation of aryl−nickel
intermediates is likely required for isomerization to allenes. It
should be noted that no self-coupling products 10 were detected

aforementioned experimental results and previous re-
search,<sup>8,10b[8][10b]</sup> we propose the following possible mechanism-
(Scheme 5D): the Ni(II) precursor is in situ reduced by zinc
powder to generate a Ni(0) intermediate (I), which undergoes
oxidative addition with aryl halides to form aryl-substituted
Ni(II) species (II). This species is then further reduced by zinc
powder to produce an Ni(I) intermediate (III). This nickel
intermediate undergoes a two-electron oxidative addition with
propargylic carbonates to form an Ni(III) intermediate (IV) .
Due to the influence of the steric hindrance surrounding the
nickel center, the Ni(III) intermediate isomerizes to form an
allenyl nickel complex (V). Subsequent reductive elimination of
the allenyl nickel complex (V) yields the final product and
regenerates the Ni(I) intermediate (VI), which is then reduced
back to Ni(0) by zinc powder, thereby completing the entire
catalytic cycle. In addition to the aforementioned catalytic cycle
involving double oxidative addition, this reaction may also
proceed via a migratory insertion mechanism<sup>12</sup> (For details on
the catalytic cycle, please refer to the Supporting Information).

controlled reductive coupling reaction between secondary
propargyl carbonates and aryl halides for the highly
regioselective synthesis of aryl-substituted allenes. This method
not only eliminates the need for arylmetal reagents in traditional
coupling processes but also overcomes the inherent structural
limitations of existing reductive coupling reactions with
propargyl electrophiles. This method exhibits excellent func-
tional group compatibility and is suitable for late-stage
modifications of complex structural products. The mechanism
reveals that this reaction does not proceed through the radical
pathway but instead follows a two-electron process. Currently,
